nodes.characterization_summary: S–Co(OH)₂, Co(OH)₂/CeO₂ and S–Co(OH)₂/CeO₂ samples show diffraction peaks at 19.1°, 32.5°, 38.0°, and 51.5° corresponding to (001), (100), (011), (002), and (012) planes of hexagonal Co(OH)₂ (PDF#74-1057). No CeO₂ phase signal detected possibly due to poor crystallinity.
nodes.evidence_snippet: According to Fig. 3b, the preparative S–Co(OH)₂, Co(OH)₂/CeO₂ and S-Co(OH)₂/CeO₂ samples show a set of distinct diffraction peaks at 19.1°, 32.5°, 38.0°, and 51.5°, which correspond to the (001), (100), (011), (002), and (012) of hexagonal crystal Co(OH)₂ (PDF#74-1057)

nodes.characterization_summary: S–Co(OH)₂/CeO₂ displays Raman signals for both Co(OH)₂ at 522 cm⁻¹ and 690 cm⁻¹, and CeO₂ at ~455 cm⁻¹. Characteristic peak at ~597 cm⁻¹ corresponds to Co-S bonding.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Notably, S–Co(OH)₂/CeO₂ displayed two sets of Raman signals include both Co(OH)₂ and CeO₂, hinting at a feasible interfacial architecture. Meanwhile, a characteristic Raman peaks at ~597 cm⁻¹ was observed, which correspond well to the Co-S

nodes.characterization_summary: S–Co(OH)₂/CeO₂ shows typical lamellar structure with loose porous morphology favorable for electrolyte moistening and bubble escape.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The microstructure was explored by field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM), as shown in Figs. 3d and S7, S-Co(OH)₂/CeO₂ shows a typical lamellar structure, the loose porous morphology is favorable for electrolyte moistening and bubble escape.

nodes.characterization_summary: Interplanar distances of 0.24 nm and 0.31 nm indexed to (011) planes of Co(OH)₂ and (111) planes of CeO₂, confirming interface structure formation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Moreover, the interplanar distances of 0.24 and 0.31 nm are indexed to the (011) planes of Co(OH)₂ and the (111) planes of CeO₂, respectively (Fig. 3e–f), confirming the formation of interface structure.

nodes.characterization_summary: EDS elemental mapping shows uniform Co and O distribution over entire surface, while Ce is locally distributed, confirming S-Co(OH)₂/CeO₂ heterostructure fabrication.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) mapping also illustrates a clear interfacial distribution. The Co and O exhibit uniform distributed over the entire surface, while the Ce is locally distributed

nodes.characterization_summary: Co 2p shows Co³⁺/Co²⁺ peaks at 780.59/781.71 eV in S–Co(OH)₂ with +0.14 eV shift and increased Co³⁺/Co²⁺ ratio in S–Co(OH)₂/CeO₂ indicating electron transfer. Ce 3d shows Ce³⁺/Ce⁴⁺ ratio increased to 0.79 from 0.55. O 1s shifted to higher binding energy indicating stronger M-O covalency. S 2p at 163.23 eV confirms Co-S bonding.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The high-resolution Co 2p spectra of S–Co(OH)₂ in Fig. 4a illustrates two peaks at 780.59 and 781.71 eV, corresponding to the Co³⁺ and Co²⁺, respectively [32,33]. The Co 2p spectra of S–Co(OH)₂/CeO₂ shows comparable characteristics to that of S–Co(OH)₂ except for slightly positive shift of +0.14 eV in binding energy, and the ratios of Co³⁺/Co²⁺ was increased

nodes.characterization_summary: d-band center (ε_d) of S–Co(OH)₂/CeO₂ located between S–Co(OH)₂ and CeO₂, illustrating interface interaction yields moderate adsorption energy of intermediates.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Figs. 4e and S12, the XPS-VB spectra shown that ε_d of S-Co(OH)₂/CeO₂ is located between S–Co(OH)₂ and CeO₂, illustrating the introducing interface interaction can yield moderate adsorption energy of intermediates

nodes.characterization_summary: Work function (Φ) values for S–Co(OH)₂ and CeO₂ calculated as 4.96 eV and 5.18 eV respectively, suggesting large ΔΦ at interface.
nodes.evidence_snippet: According to Fig. 4f, the calculated Φ values for S–Co(OH)₂ and CeO2 were 4.96 and 5.18 eV, respectively, suggesting a relatively large ΔΦ at the S–Co(OH)₂/CeO₂ interface.

nodes.characterization_summary: In-situ Raman shows Co(OH)₂ peak at ~530 cm⁻¹ initially, new CoOOH peak at ~495 cm⁻¹ above 1.3 V, and Co(IV)-O signal at ~570 cm⁻¹ at 1.4 V indicating fast surface reconstruction.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Fig. 6i, initially the characteristic peak at ~530 cm⁻¹ can be assigned to Co(OH)₂. By raising the voltage over 1.3 V, a new characteristic peaks at ~495 cm⁻¹ can be observed, which corresponded to the CoOOH, and the low switched voltage also indicates a fast surface reconstruction.

nodes.characterization_summary: In-situ XPS Co 2p shows shift from ~780.8 eV (Co²⁺) at 1.023 V to ~779.7 eV (Co³⁺) at 1.423 V confirming phase transformation to S-CoOOH. At higher potentials >1.723 V, Co valence state stabilizes unlike S–Co(OH)₂, indicating CeO₂ prevents over-oxidation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Fig. 6j, the peak located at ~780.8 eV of Co 2p spectrum corresponds to Co²⁺ at initial voltage 1.023 V, which is well assigned to Co(OH)₂. When the applied voltage reaches about 1.423 V, the oxidation state of the surface have changed significantly, the peak position of Co 2p shows a significant negative shift to ~779.7 eV

nodes.characterization_summary: ICP-MS shows only slight Co dissolution for S–Co(OH)₂/CeO₂ during OER compared to large amount from S–Co(OH)₂, indicating CeO₂ suppresses Co over-oxidation and dissolution.
nodes.evidence_snippet: As shown in Fig. 6g, a large amount of Co in S–Co(OH)₂ was dissolved into the electrolyte during OER process, while only slightly dissolved was observed for S–Co(OH)₂/CeO₂, suggesting that the introduction of electron-rich CeO₂ can suppress over-oxidation of S–Co(OH)₂ and slow down the dissolution of Co ions
